# Field-effect transistor on oxidised silicon (MOSFET) (`mosfet`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs semiconductors_transistor, semiconductor_purification; helped by integrated_circuit
- Core idea: The simplest amplifier idea is a capacitor: a metal plate (gate) separated by a thin insulator from a semiconductor, where a voltage on the gate attracts carriers into a thin channel under it and so switches a current between two contacts (source and drain) with almost no input current. It failed for decades because charges trapped at the crystal surface screen the field. The cure is to heat clean silicon to about 1,000 °C in oxygen or steam: it grows a tight glassy layer of its own oxide that ties up the surface states and serves as the gate insulator. Pairing an n-channel with a p-channel device (CMOS) gives logic that draws most of its dynamic power while switching and also has leakage current at rest. This device, not the junction transistor, is the one made by the thousand million on every chip.
- Pitfalls:
  - Trying it on germanium, whose oxide dissolves in water; the stable oxide is the reason silicon won
  - Sodium contamination from glassware, sweat and chemicals: mobile ions in the oxide make the devices drift, which held MOS back until the mid-1960s
  - Static charge from a hand punctures the thin gate oxide
  - Dismissing it because it is slower than a junction transistor, as Bell Labs did in 1960; its simplicity and small size matter more
- History: europe: 1934 – Oskar Heil's British patent for a field-effect device; americas: 1926 – Lilienfeld's field-effect patent application; 1945–1947 Shockley's field-effect experiments fail, Bardeen explains it by surface states; 1955–1958 Frosch and Derick, then Atalla, study oxide on silicon at Bell Labs; 1959–1960 Atalla and Kahng's MOS transistor; 1963 Wanlass and Sah's CMOS (Fairchild)
- Read:
  - Ross Knox Bassett, To the Digital Age: Research Labs, Start-up Companies, and the Rise of MOS Technology (2002)
  - Michael Riordan & Lillian Hoddeson, Crystal Fire: The Birth of the Information Age (1997)
